items.name: The leaky bucket method
items.explanation: Each request adds to a counter, and the counter drains at a steady rate. A request is refused when the counter would overflow, so traffic comes out at the steady rate while short bursts are absorbed.

assumedBy.quote: The leaky bucket algorithm allows a great level of accuracy while being nicer on resources (this is what the stock NGINX module is using).

items.name: Memcached
items.explanation: A memory-only cache that many servers can share. You store and fetch values by key, and it offers a few simple operations such as get, set and an atomic increment.

assumedBy.quote: So the situation was that the only operations available were GET, SET and INCR (atomic increment).

items.name: Redis
items.explanation: An in-memory data store, often used as a shared cache or counter store. Answers are fast, and the data lives on whatever machine runs it.

assumedBy.quote: Back in early 2023, the existing Ratelimit infrastructure at Databricks consisted of an Envoy ingress gateway making calls to the Ratelimit Service, with a single instance of Redis backing the service

sources.title: Get started with Redis Open Source

items.name: Envoy and the ingress gateway
items.explanation: Envoy is a proxy that sits in front of services and handles traffic for them. An ingress gateway is the one at the edge of a system that all outside requests pass through first.

assumedBy.quote: consisted of an Envoy ingress gateway making calls to the Ratelimit Service

items.name: Single point of failure
items.explanation: One part whose failure takes the whole system down. The usual fix is a standby that can take over.

assumedBy.quote: Redis as a single point of failure - Our single Redis instance was our single point of failure, and we had to do something about that.
